title: Effective polynomial simulation of Extended Frege by Resolution
formal: Do there exist a deterministic transformation R and fixed polynomials p,q such that, for every propositional formula F and every integer \(s\ge 1, R\)(F,1ˢ) outputs a CNF formula in at most p(|F|+s) bit operations, F is a tautology if and only if R(F,1ˢ) is unsatisfiable, and whenever F has an Extended Frege proof of length at most s, R(F,1ˢ) has a Resolution refutation of length at most q(|F|+s)?
why: Determines whether allowing efficient preprocessing fundamentally changes the apparent gap between elementary clause reasoning and proof systems that can name arbitrary intermediate Boolean computations. This affects what proof-size separations say about algorithms for finding proofs.

progress.text: Pitassi and Santhanam define effective polynomial simulation and explicitly pose the Resolution-versus-Extended-Frege question.
Regular and unrestricted Resolution are shown equivalent under effective simulations, with the auxiliary proof-size parameter retained.

definitions:
A propositional formula uses Boolean variables, negation \(
eg\) and implication →, with the usual truth tables; other connectives are fixed abbreviations. A tautology is true under every Boolean assignment. A literal is a variable or its negation, a clause is a disjunction of literals, and a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. The empty clause is false. A Resolution refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each line being an input clause or the resolvent \(C\lor D\) of earlier clauses \(C\lor x\) and \(D\lor 
eg x\). Lines can be reused, so the proof is a directed acyclic derivation, not necessarily a tree. Fix Extended Frege as follows: ordinary Frege lines are substitution instances of \(A	o (B	o A), (A	o (B	o C))	o ((A	o B)	o (A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o 
eg A)	o (A	o B)\), or follow by modus ponens from A and \(A	o B\). One may also introduce an extension axiom \(z\leftrightarrow B\), where z is fresh, does not occur in the target F, and B uses only original variables and previously introduced extension variables. Here \(z\leftrightarrow B\) abbreviates \((z	o B)\land (B	o z)\). The final line is F, containing no extension variables. Formulas, proofs and line references have explicit finite binary encodings; length counts the whole encoding. Standard alternative Frege bases and symbol-count conventions are polynomially equivalent. The input 1ˢ is a unary string, so the permitted time is polynomial in s, not log s. The transformation receives F and s but no EF proof. It must preserve the tautology/unsatisfiability equivalence for every F and every s, even if s is smaller than the shortest proof or F is not a tautology. Only the short-Resolution-refutation guarantee is conditional on an EF proof of length at most s. Resolution is represented by refuting a CNF, while Frege proves a tautology; this explicitly implements the source’s comparison of proof systems over their natural encodings.
answer_criterion: Prove or refute the existence of R,p,q satisfying all these conditions. The requested notion is effective polynomial simulation as in Definition 2.5 of the source. A polynomial procedure that converts a supplied EF proof is an additional, stronger guarantee and is not required. A lower bound on Resolution proofs of the original untransformed formula alone does not refute this claim.

context_blocks.title: Can preprocessing change the proof-size comparison?
context_blocks.text: Resolution is a basic way to certify that a set of clauses is inconsistent. Extended Frege additionally uses named intermediate formulas, allowing compact reuse of complicated expressions. The question asks whether a uniformly efficient transformation of the statement can make Resolution proofs as short, up to a polynomial, as EF proofs.

context_blocks.title: A Resolution step
context_blocks.text: From \(x\lor y\) and \(\neg x\), Resolution derives y. Together with the clause \(\neg y\), it then derives the empty clause and certifies inconsistency. Larger derivations reuse earlier clauses. An extension variable, by contrast, can name a compound formula and be reused wherever that formula is needed.

context_blocks.title: Why the extra input matters
context_blocks.text: The transformation is given a proposed proof-size allowance s. It may spend polynomial time in that allowance, even if the statement itself is short. It must preserve correctness for all allowances, but it needs to guarantee a short output refutation only when an EF proof fits within the allowance. The actual proof is never supplied to it.

context_blocks.title: The known separation answers a different comparison
context_blocks.text: Ordinary polynomial simulation compares proofs of the same statement. Known Resolution lower bounds rule out ordinary simulation of Extended Frege. Effective simulation allows the statement to change through a correctness-preserving transformation, so those lower bounds do not automatically answer this question.

context_blocks.title: A later example of the distinction
context_blocks.text: Buss and Yolcu show that regular Resolution effectively simulates unrestricted Resolution, despite known exponential separations when both systems must use the same formula. Regular Resolution forbids resolving a variable twice along a derivation path. Their result demonstrates that the distinction has mathematical force, but does not provide an effective simulation of EF.

sentences: Resolution refutes inconsistent clauses, while Extended Frege permits named intermediate Boolean formulas.
Ordinary proof-size comparisons keep the statement fixed and separate these systems.
This question allows a polynomial-time transformation of the statement, given a unary bound on an EF proof’s length.
Whenever that bound is sufficient, the transformed CNF must have a comparably short Resolution refutation, while correctness must be preserved for every input.
An answer would clarify whether efficient preprocessing can overcome the proof-size gap between these systems.
